lead: Two springs can be nested, one inside the other, so that a large load fits in a small space and the set still works if one spring breaks. Railway buffers, heavy-duty valve trains and governors use such concentric springs. Many springs also work under a load that rises and falls millions of times, so they fail by fatigue long before the static stress is reached. This chapter shows how nested springs share a load and how a spring is checked for a fluctuating load.
prereq: You need the stress and deflection formulas of helical compression springs, and the Goodman and Soderberg lines from the chapter on fluctuating stresses.

blocks.text: Two springs of the same free length placed one inside the other are compressed by the same amount: they act in parallel. So their rates add and the load divides in the ratio of the rates:

blocks.where: P₁ and P₂ are the loads on the outer and inner spring in N; k₁ and k₂ their rates in N/mm; the set's rate is k₁ + k₂.

blocks.text: The two springs are wound in opposite hands, one right-hand and one left-hand, so that a coil of one cannot slip between the coils of the other and jam the set.

The standard design assumes both springs are of the same material, have the same free length, the same solid length, the same spring index C and the same maximum stress. Since τ = K·8PC/(πd²) with the same K and C, the load each carries is proportional to d²:

blocks.where: d₁ and d₂ are the wire diameters of the outer and inner springs.

blocks.text: The radial clearance between the springs is usually taken as half the difference of the wire diameters, c = (d₁ − d₂)/2. Writing the clearance as (D₁ − d₁)/2 − (D₂ + d₂)/2 with D = Cd gives d₁/d₂ = C/(C − 2). Equal solid lengths of the active coils need N₁d₁ = N₂d₂.
A spring in a valve train or clutch is loaded between P<sub>min</sub> and P<sub>max</sub> again and again. Split the load into a mean part and an alternating part:
P<sub>m</sub> is the mean load; the alternating load is P<sub>a</sub> = (P<sub>max</sub> − P<sub>min</sub>)/2.

Indian textbooks such as Bhandari apply only the direct-shear factor K<sub>s</sub> = 1 + 0.5/C to the mean stress and the full Wahl factor K to the alternating stress, because the curvature effect behaves like a stress concentration, which matters only for the fluctuating part. Shigley applies the curvature factor to both, which is a little more cautious. Follow your prescribed book.
τ<sub>m</sub> is the mean shear stress; the alternating shear stress is τ<sub>a</sub> = K·8P<sub>a</sub>D/(πd³).

S<sub>se</sub> is the torsional endurance limit of the wire (from data or given); S<sub>su</sub> the torsional ultimate strength, about 0.67S<sub>ut</sub>; n the factor of safety. Using the torsional yield strength S<sub>sy</sub> (about 0.45S<sub>ut</sub> for cold-drawn wire) in place of S<sub>su</sub> gives the safer Soderberg line.

Some textbooks build the line from the spring's pulsating test, through (S<sub>se</sub>′/2, S<sub>se</sub>′/2) to (S<sub>sy</sub>, 0); use it when your book does. Shot peening leaves the wire surface in compression and raises S<sub>se</sub>; presetting (closing the new spring to solid once) lets it carry higher stress without taking a set.

examples.question: Two concentric springs of spring steel carry a total load of 10 kN with a deflection of about 80 mm. Both have spring index 6 and permissible shear stress 600 MPa; G = 81 370 MPa. Find the wire and coil diameters, the load on each, the clearance and the active coils.
steps: Outer coils: N₁ = Gd₁⁴δ/(8P₁D₁³) = 81 370 × 15⁴ × 80/(8 × 6923 × 90³) = 8.16; take 8. Inner: N₂ = 12.24; take 12, so N₁d₁ = N₂d₂ = 120 mm.
Rates: k₁ = 88.3 N/mm, k₂ = 39.2 N/mm; set deflection 10 000/127.5 = 78.4 mm; loads 6923 N and 3077 N as planned.
examples.answer: Outer 15 mm wire on 90 mm mean diameter with 8 active coils (6.92 kN); inner 10 mm wire on 60 mm with 12 active coils (3.08 kN); clearance 2.5 mm; deflection 78.4 mm.

examples.question: A spring of d = 10 mm and D = 80 mm works between 500 N and 1500 N. The wire has S<sub>ut</sub> = 1400 MPa and a torsional endurance limit S<sub>se</sub> = 310 MPa. Find the factor of safety by the Goodman line, using K<sub>s</sub> for the mean stress and K for the alternating stress.
steps: P<sub>m</sub> = 1000 N, P<sub>a</sub> = 500 N; 8D/(πd³) = 640/3141.6 = 0.2037 per newton.
With K on both parts (Shigley), τ<sub>m</sub> = 241.2 MPa and n = 1.55; with S<sub>sy</sub> = 630 MPa (Soderberg), n = 1.36.
examples.answer: n = 1.61 by Goodman with K<sub>s</sub> on the mean stress (1.55 if K is used on both).

traps: Splitting the load equally between nested springs. They share the deflection, so the load divides as k₁ : k₂ (here 2.25 : 1).
Adding deflections of nested springs. Deflections add only for springs in series; nested springs add rates.
Winding both springs the same hand. Coils can then interlock and jam.
Comparing shear stresses with tensile strengths. Use the torsional values S<sub>se</sub>, S<sub>su</sub>, S<sub>sy</sub>.
Mixing the two stress-factor conventions in one answer. State which one you use.

quiz.q: Two nested springs have rates 40 and 25 N/mm. What is the rate of the set?
Why are concentric springs wound in opposite hands?
quiz.a: So that the coils of one cannot screw into the gaps of the other and lock the set, especially if one breaks.

quiz.q: Why does shot peening raise the fatigue strength of a spring?
quiz.a: It leaves a layer of compressive residual stress at the wire surface, where fatigue cracks start, so a crack must first overcome that compression.

quiz.q: A nested set of 45 and 15 N/mm carries 6 kN. Find the deflection and the load on each spring.
A spring has τ<sub>m</sub> = 200 MPa and τ<sub>a</sub> = 100 MPa with S<sub>se</sub> = 300 and S<sub>su</sub> = 900 MPa. Find the Goodman factor of safety.
In the first worked example the outer spring has 10 total coils and the inner 14 (two end coils each). Which goes solid first, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: Solid lengths are 10 × 15 = 150 mm and 14 × 10 = 140 mm. With the same free length the outer spring reaches solid first, after 10 mm less travel. The set's travel must stop before that, or the outer spring is crushed solid and the stress jumps.

beyond: Not for the exam. Racing valve trains use two or three nested springs plus a damper to fight surge at high engine speed. Modern fatigue data for spring wire come from standards such as EN 10270, and finite-element models check coil clash between nested springs. Search for nested valve springs and spring presetting.

figure.caption: The concentric pair of the first worked example in section. Both springs have index 6 and are squeezed the same 78.4 mm, so the 10 kN load splits in the ratio of their rates, 6.92 kN to 3.08 kN, and both wires reach the same 589 MPa. The 2.5 mm gap keeps the coils from rubbing.
